chapter: Complaints to Senator Eastland, FCC and WDSU
title: Newspaper item on a contempt case and La Rocca's 1957 letter to Eastland
summary: An article on the WDSU director's appeal is read, then La Rocca's 1957 letter asking for a law requiring scripts and listing fourteen exhibits.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: I want you to read this here about a nine-man court.

This is a nine-man court to hear appeal of Live Right from the New Orleans States Washington Bureau. They go on Washington. The appeal of Herman Live Right, former New Orleans television station director, from a contempt of Congress conviction, will be heard by the full nine-man United States Court of Appeals here, April 19... I'm sorry, April 23rd. The Live Right case, one of nine in a mass, but not consolidated hearing, will be taken up by the court at 10 a.m. Live Right and Allen bond were sentenced to three months in a prison in order to pay a $500 bond by U.S. Judge Richmond B. Keats more than a year ago after a jury had found him guilty on all 14 counts of an indictment charging contempt of Congress. The former WDSU television program director, 46, was accused of willfully refusing to answer questions asked him by the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee during an investigation of communism in the New Orleans. Other appeals will be heard from playwright Arthur Miller, newspaper man Robert Smelton, and William A. Price, John T. Gojack, Fort Wayne, Indiana labor leader, Norton Anthony Russell, engineer from Yellow Springs, Ohio, Bernard Deutsch, former student at the University of Pennsylvania, and Goldie Watson, Washington Dress Shoppe, owner. That's the end of the article. Another letter? Yeah. I think it's going on. Now this is a letter. D. James, Nick LaRocca, 2218 Constance Street, New Orleans, Louisiana, 13 February the 10th, 1957. Senator J.O. Eastland of Mississippi, Washington, D.C. Honorable Senator Eastland, the purpose of this letter is first to thank you for the conviction of Herman Leveride and to ask you to introduce a bill in Congress for a law to make it compulsory for television and radio stations to furnish a script. See, that was to make it compulsory for television and radio stations to furnish a script as to the programs they put on the air. This station, WDSU, has put on a program of lies against me and the ODJB. The two letters attached to this will tell my story. How can I sue them? They refused to furnish me with script of the program. I'm a poor man. I could not have the programs monitored. I'm sorry, that says, I could not have all their programs monitored. Making this law so that the owners of these stations would be responsible for what their personnel would say over the air to blacken any one name with statements that were not true. Most of this supposed history on jazz was written in the last 10 to 15 years by muddleheads, jug-toters, left-wingers, and pro-necro writers who derive grants from the Guggenheimer Foundation, NAACP, Will Handy, Chicago Defender, and people who exploit this music for monetary gain and self-aggrandizement. We have two such people in New Orleans, Ms. Myra Menville, Dr. Edmond Sushon, who operate the New Orleans Jazz Club, selling jazz periodicals, VIVS, the second line, All Negro Writings and Lies, read this jazz music as these people were not around when the ODJB was making history. Some months back, this bunch was having mixed bands playing from the same bandstand with white men. This had been going on for several years, which is purely practicing integration. They have gone underground now as I have written this. Ms. Myra Menville several letters ready to sing. Your Honor, I have included some photostatic copies that you may not think of me as some crime, but these documents will tell the truth. That's example one, Chicago. Chicago. Yes. Example two, opening in New York City, rising weather. example three, is that exhibit or example? Exhibit. Exhibit. I'm sorry. Exhibit three, first jazz record by the Victor Company, March 7, 1917. Exhibit four, Winter Garden, New York. Example five. Exhibit. Exhibit, I'm sorry. Exhibit five, theaters around New York City. Exhibit six, editorial, Times-Picayune, June 20th, 1918. Shows how little this new audience knew about this music. Exhibit seven, London, England. Exhibit eight, Call Kitchen, New York City. Exhibit nine, Entertaining Soldiers, Marines and Sailors, First World War. Exhibit ten, Music Trades. Exhibit eleven, Nickel Rocker by Thomas E. Wynn Dabney. Exhibit twelve, New Owners Association of Commerce. Exhibit thirteen, Vixcuro letter. Exhibit fourteen, Remoulade by Howard Jacobs. This write-up came about from the editor of Reader's Digest who asked Mr. Jacobs to find out about me, whether I was still living and what I was doing. Later he mentioned me in the column Periscoping the News. Hoping you will have time to bring this matter before the Congress. Some kind of throttle will be put on these untrue programs. Thanking you in advance, I am sincerely yours, Leader and Manager, Original Dixieland Jazz Band, now in retirement at sixty-eight years.
